title: O For that warning voice ... Woe to the inhabitants on Earth
short: The narrator wishes that the warning cry heard by John in Revelation 12 could sound now, before Satan reaches Adam and Eve.
body: The book opens with the narrator's wish that the voice which John ('he who saw Th' Apocalyps') heard cry 'Woe to the inhabitants on Earth!' might warn our first parents in time. Verity identifies the text: 'Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath' (Revelation 12:12), spoken when 'the Dragon', the old serpent, is cast out of heaven. 'Apocalypse' means an uncovering. Satan comes 'first Tempter ere Accuser', Verity notes, for the devil is called 'the accuser of our brethren' (Revelation 12:10), and the Greek diabolos means 'slanderer'. The opening sets the tense of the book: everything beautiful in Eden is seen with foreknowledge of its loss.

title: Satan's soliloquy on Niphates: 'Which way I flie is Hell; my self am Hell'
short: Alone, Satan admits that God was good, that he fell freely, and that he carries Hell within him; but pride forbids repentance.
body: Addressing the sun (4.32-113), Satan confesses what he concealed from his followers: God 'deservd no such return', he himself 'Chose freely' to fall, and Heaven's 'free Love' is not to blame. Verity records the tradition, from Milton's nephew Edward Phillips, that lines 32-41 were written early (around 1642) as the opening of a projected tragedy on the Fall, and Addison thought this the finest of Satan's speeches. 'Which way I flie is Hell; my self am Hell' completes the boast of 1.254-55 that 'The mind is its own place': the Dartmouth edition compares Mephistophilis in Doctor Faustus, 'where we are is hell'. Satan considers repentance but finds 'no place Left for Repentance' (Hebrews 12:17, of Esau), because submission is a word 'Disdain forbids me'. The speech makes him tragic as well as villainous.

title: Evil be thou my Good
short: Satan's deliberate inversion of values, the moment he chooses evil knowingly; it fulfils Isaiah's woe on those who 'call evil good, and good evil'.
body: The soliloquy ends in a decision: 'So farewel Hope, and with Hope farewel Fear, Farewel Remorse: all Good to me is lost; Evil be thou my Good'. Satan now chooses evil as his good, the inversion condemned by Isaiah, 'Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil' (Isaiah 5:20). Verity notes that 'by thee' is repeated for emphasis, and that Satan claims to divide empire with God, ruling 'more then half' since Hell and the new world will be his. The Dartmouth edition points to the corollary in Book IX, 'all good to me becomes Bane' (9.122-23). The passions that cross his face during the speech, 'ire, envie and despair', disfigure his borrowed cherub's form, which is how Uriel, watching from the sun, detects him (4.114-30).

title: Mozambic ... Sabean Odours from the spicie shoare Of Arabie the blest
short: Eden's fragrance meets Satan like the spice-scented winds that greet sailors off Mozambique from Arabia the blessed.
body: As Satan approaches Paradise, its perfumed air is compared to the scents that sailors rounding the Cape of Good Hope and passing Mozambique smell on the north-east wind from 'Sabea', biblical Sheba, in 'Arabie the blest' (Arabia Felix, the fertile south of the peninsula, modern Yemen). Verity explains the classical name and the commonplace of Arabian spices; the Dartmouth edition notes that the image continues the language of the spice trade used for Satan's flight at 2.636-42, and that the sailors' 'Cape of Hope' is ironic for one who is past hope. Diodorus Siculus (3.46) describes such fragrance carried far out to sea from the Arabian coast. Satan, the trader-voyager, comes to the garden as to a rich market.

title: Asmodeus with the fishie fume
short: The demon of the Book of Tobit, driven from Sara by the smell of burning fish when Raphael guided Tobias: a comic contrast to Eden's perfume.
body: Satan likes the scent of Eden 'better then Asmodeus' liked the 'fishie fume' that drove him away. Verity summarises the apocryphal Book of Tobit: the demon Asmodeus, in love with Sara, killed her seven husbands on their wedding nights; the angel Raphael, travelling in disguise with young Tobias, told him to burn the heart and liver of a fish, and the smell drove the demon 'into the utmost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him' (Tobit 8:3). Verity notes the Hebrew form Ashmedai, 'destroyer', and that Milton calls him Asmadai in 6.365. The allusion prepares for Raphael's visit to Adam in Book V, where he is called 'the sociable Spirit, that deign'd To travel with Tobias' (5.221-23), and links Satan's coming to a demon of lust and destruction.

title: a prowling Wolfe ... So clomb this first grand Thief into Gods Fould
short: Satan leaps the wall of Paradise like a wolf into a sheepfold or a thief through a window: the false shepherds of John 10 and Milton's 'lewd Hirelings'.
body: Scorning the gate, Satan overleaps the wall 'at one slight bound'. Two similes follow: a wolf leaping into a fold, and a burglar climbing in at the window or over the tiles. Verity cites the parable of the Good Shepherd: 'He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber' (John 10:1). The narrator then adds: 'So since into his Church lewd Hirelings climbe' (4.193). Verity explains the reference to Milton's tract on 'The Likeliest Means to Remove Hirelings out of the Church' (1659), against paid clergy, and compares the attack on greedy shepherds in Lycidas. The Dartmouth edition notes the awkward questions the similes raise about how well the garden is guarded.

title: Sat like a Cormorant on the Tree of Life
short: Satan perches on the Tree of Life in the shape of a greedy sea-bird, using the tree of immortality only as a lookout.
body: Satan flies to the Tree of Life, 'the middle Tree and highest there', and sits on it 'like a Cormorant', a voracious bird of prey, symbolic of greed; Verity notes the bird's associations and its appearance in English versions of Isaiah 34:11. The narrator comments that he 'thought not on the virtue of that life-giving Plant, but only us'd For prospect, what well us'd had bin the pledge Of immortalitie'. Verity wonders what proper use Satan could have made of it, and suggests the passage implies the possibility of a spiritual renewal he refuses. The episode states a principle the poem repeats: the good things of creation are perverted by misuse, 'so little knows Any, but God alone, to value right The good before him'. The Tree of Life stands, as in Genesis 2:9, beside the Tree of Knowledge.

title: Eden's bounds: Auran, Seleucia, Telassar
short: Milton fixes Eden between Hauran in Syria and Seleucia on the Tigris, where the 'children of Eden' lived in Telassar (2 Kings 19:12).
body: Eden is the region; Paradise is the garden planted 'eastward in Eden' (Genesis 2:8), as Verity, quoting Masson, distinguishes. Milton marks the region's limits from 'Auran' (Hauran, a district south of Damascus, named in Ezekiel 47:16-18 as a border of Israel) east to 'the Royal Towrs Of great Seleucia, built by Grecian Kings', the Seleucid capital on the Tigris near modern Baghdad, founded by Alexander's general Seleucus about 312 BC. Telassar is where 'the children of Eden' dwelt, according to 2 Kings 19:12 and Isaiah 37:12; Verity cites a commentary placing them on the Euphrates. Milton thus anchors the mythical garden in the historical geography of Mesopotamia, with the Tigris, flowing underground beneath the mount of Paradise, as the river that waters it (4.223-35).

title: Hesperian Fables true, If true, here onely
short: The golden apples of the Hesperides: the classical myth is true only of Eden, if it is true at all.
body: The fruit trees of Paradise bear 'Fruit burnisht with Golden Rinde', so that the narrator comments: 'Hesperian Fables true, If true, here onely'. The Hesperides were nymphs of the evening who, with a serpent, guarded a tree of golden apples in a garden at the western edge of the world (Hesiod, Theogony 215-16; Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.637-48), which Hercules stole. Verity glosses the clause: the stories of the Hesperian apples would be true only of this place, if at all. The double qualification is characteristic of Milton's handling of pagan myth: it may preserve a distorted memory of Eden, but it remains fable. The myth's own details, a guarded tree of golden fruit, a serpent, and a theft, make the comparison quietly ominous.

title: Universal Pan Knit with the Graces and the Hours
short: Pan, god of nature (his name read as 'all'), dances with the Graces and the Seasons: Eden lives in an eternal spring.
body: The birds sing and the leaves tremble while 'Universal Pan Knit with the Graces and the Hours in dance Led on th' Eternal Spring'. Verity explains that Pan, god of shepherds, was taken as god of all nature because his name resembles Greek pan, 'all'; the Graces (Charites) personified beauty and joy, and the Hours (Horae) the seasons, whose round was imagined as a dance. The allegory says that in Eden there is one season only, spring; Verity notes Milton's Latin elegy on the coming of spring and suggests a painting such as Botticelli's Primavera, which the Dartmouth edition also mentions. In the Nativity Ode Milton had made Christ the true 'mighty Pan', so the pagan figure here is both decorative and a type of the Creator's presence in nature.

title: Proserpin gathring flours ... her self a fairer Floure
short: Not Enna, where Proserpina was carried off by Dis while gathering flowers, could rival Eden: a 'negative simile' that foreshadows Eve's fate.
body: The first of a series of negative comparisons ('Not that faire field Of Enna...') denies that any famous paradise of legend equals Eden. In the myth, Proserpina was gathering flowers at Enna in Sicily when 'gloomie Dis' (Pluto, god of the underworld) seized her, causing her mother Ceres to search the whole world (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.385-424; Fasti 4.419-62, which Verity cites). The comparison is famous for its pathos and its foreshadowing: Eve too will be found among her flowers, 'her self, though fairest unsupported Flour', by the infernal power (9.432, which Verity notes echoes this line), and her loss will bring death and the change of seasons into the world. Verity and the Dartmouth edition note the scansion 'Prosérpin' and the 'negative simile' technique.

title: Daphne by Orontes; the Nyseian Ile; Amalthea and Young Bacchus
short: Other famous gardens that cannot rival Eden: Apollo's grove of Daphne near Antioch, and the island of Nysa where Ammon hid the infant Bacchus.
body: The 'sweet Grove Of Daphne by Orontes' was a laurel and cypress grove near Antioch in Syria, sacred to Apollo, with an oracle and a spring named after the Castalian spring of Delphi (Verity, quoting Keightley); the name recalls Ovid's Daphne, who escaped Apollo by becoming a laurel. The 'Nyseian Ile Girt with the River Triton' alludes to a story in Diodorus Siculus (3.67-70): the Libyan king Ammon, 'whom Gentiles Ammon call and Libyan Jove', hid his mistress Amalthea and their 'Florid Son Young Bacchus' on the island of Nysa from his wife Rhea. The Dartmouth edition adds that Renaissance mythographers identified Ammon with Noah's son Ham, so that pagan story is again rooted in biblical history. Each garden is a place of illicit love or pursuit, quietly contrasted with Eden's innocence.

title: Abassin Kings ... Mount Amara
short: A mountain in Abyssinia where the emperor's sons were kept confined, thought by some to be the true site of Paradise.
body: The last rival is Mount Amara in Abyssinia (Ethiopia), 'though this by som suppos'd True Paradise under the Ethiop Line', that is, on the equator. Verity quotes Heylyn's Cosmography, Milton's likely source: on its summit stood palaces in which the younger sons of the Abyssinian emperor were confined to prevent rebellion, and its temperate air led some to think it was the place of Paradise. Verity adds that Samuel Johnson used the same tradition for the 'happy valley' of Rasselas (1759). 'Amara' is properly Amhara, a range rather than a single peak. The image of a royal paradise that is also a prison makes an apt last term in the series of false Edens before the description turns to Adam and Eve.

anchor: Hee for God only, shee for God in him
title: Hee for God only, shee for God in him
short: The first description of Adam and Eve states a hierarchy of the sexes, drawn from Paul, that has been fiercely debated by modern readers.
body: Adam and Eve are both made in God's image and share 'true filial freedom', yet they are 'Not equal, as thir sex not equal seemd; For contemplation hee and valour formd, For softness shee and sweet attractive Grace, Hee for God only, shee for God in him'. Milton draws on Paul: 'the head of the woman is the man' (1 Corinthians 11:3, 7-9), which Verity cites for Eve's 'subjection'. The Dartmouth edition surveys the large critical debate, from readings of the poem as straightforwardly patriarchal to defences of Eve's dignity by Diane McColley and analyses by Mary Nyquist and James Grantham Turner. Note how much depends on 'seemd': the description is focalised through Satan, who is watching, and Eve's later account of her own creation (4.440-91) complicates the hierarchy.

title: Hyacinthin Locks; sweet reluctant amorous delay
short: Adam's curling hair is 'hyacinthine', a Homeric epithet; Eve's yielding is 'sweet reluctant amorous delay', a line built on oxymoron.
body: Adam's 'Hyacinthin Locks' hang in clusters to his shoulders but no lower. Verity identifies Homer's simile for Odysseus' hair, curling 'like the hyacinth flower' (Odyssey 6.231); the Dartmouth edition adds Ovid's Hyacinthus, Apollo's beloved, and Venus' gift of flowing locks to Aeneas (Aeneid 1.589-91). The hair lengths follow 1 Corinthians 11:14-15, where long hair is a woman's glory and a covering; Verity notes that some readers see a glance at the long hair of Cavaliers. Eve's 'golden tresses' fall 'Dissheveld' like vine tendrils, implying 'subjection, but requir'd with gentle sway', yielded 'with coy submission, modest pride, And sweet reluctant amorous delay' (4.310-11). Verity notes the slow rhythm of that line and its oxymorons; the Dartmouth note observes how the description places Adam's beauty in his head and Eve's in her whole form.

anchor: A Shape within the watry gleam
title: Eve at the pool: A Shape within the watry gleam
short: Eve's first memory is of falling in love with her own reflection, a rewriting of Ovid's Narcissus that is interrupted by a divine voice.
body: Eve recalls waking beside a lake and bending over it to see 'A Shape within the watry gleam' that returned her looks 'with answering looks Of sympathie and love'. The scene, as the Dartmouth edition notes, rewrites Ovid's Narcissus, who pined away for his own reflection (Metamorphoses 3.402-510); Eve says she 'had fixt Mine eyes till now, and pin'd with vain desire', echoing his fate. A voice warns her, 'What there thou seest fair Creature is thy self', and leads her to Adam, 'whose image thou art'. Critics have read the episode very differently: as evidence of a vanity that prepares the Fall, as a natural first stage of self-knowledge, or as a lesson in moving from image to relationship. Eve at first prefers the 'smooth watry image' to Adam, 'less winning soft' (4.478-80), and turns back before being won.

title: Uriel on a Sun beam; Gabriel at the gate
short: Uriel glides down a sunbeam to warn Gabriel, commander of the guard at Eden's eastern gate, that an evil spirit has entered.
body: At sunset Uriel slides 'on a Sun beam, swift as a shooting Starr' to the eastern gate of Paradise, where Gabriel commands the angelic guard. He reports that a spirit who seemed zealous for God's works revealed 'passions foul' once he reached the mount north of Eden (4.124-30, 569-72). Verity notes that in Scripture Gabriel is a messenger (Daniel 8-9; Luke 1:19, 26), while Milton, following some tradition, makes him a warrior second only to Michael (6.44-46); the Dartmouth edition gives his place among the four archangels of Hebrew tradition. Uriel then returns 'slope downward' on the same beam to the sun, now set: the narrator pauses over whether the sun has sunk or the earth turned (4.592-97), an instance of the poem's careful neutrality between Ptolemaic and Copernican systems.

title: More lovely then Pandora ... the unwiser Son Of Japhet
short: Eve is compared to Pandora, the first woman of Greek myth, whose gift-laden beauty brought misery on mankind: 'too like In sad event'.
body: In the bridal bower Eve is lovelier than Pandora, 'whom the Gods Endowd with all thir gifts'. Verity tells the myth: Prometheus stole Zeus' fire for mankind, and Zeus in revenge had a woman made, endowed by all the gods (Greek pan + dôra, 'all gifts'), and sent by Hermes to Prometheus' brother Epimetheus, 'the unwiser Son', who took her in; she released the evils of the world (Hesiod, Works and Days 60-105; Theogony 570-612). Milton identifies the Titan Iapetus, father of Prometheus and Epimetheus, with Noah's son Japhet, as Verity and the Dartmouth edition note, in keeping with the idea that Greek myth descends from Genesis. The comparison praises Eve while ominously predicting her role, 'O too like In sad event'.

title: Haile wedded Love, mysterious Law
short: Milton's hymn to married sexual love before the Fall, attacking hypocritical praise of celibacy and the 'Court Amours' of his own day.
body: Milton insists, against much theological tradition, that Adam and Eve made love before the Fall: Eve did not refuse 'the Rites Mysterious of connubial Love', and only 'Hypocrites austerely talk Of puritie' (4.743-47). The Dartmouth edition notes the allusion to Paul's 'great mystery' of marriage (Ephesians 5:31-32) and to 1 Timothy 4:1-3, where forbidding marriage is a doctrine of devils; 'the bed is undefil'd' quotes Hebrews 13:4. The hymn, 'Haile wedded Love, mysterious Law, true source Of human ofspring', contrasts marriage with 'the bought smile Of Harlots', 'Court Amours, Mixt Dance, or wanton Mask, or Midnight Bal' (4.765-68). Verity reads the attack on court amours as a glance at Charles II's court, and the 'starv'd Lover' serenading his 'proud fair' as a parody of Cavalier love poetry.

title: Ithuriel and Zephon
greek: Hebrew names glossed 'discovery of God' and 'searcher'
short: Two cherubs sent to search the garden; their names fit their task, and Ithuriel's spear reveals Satan's true form.
body: Gabriel sends Ithuriel and Zephon to search the garden. Neither name is biblical for an angel; Verity glosses Ithuriel as 'the discovery of God' and Zephon as 'a looking out', names suited to their errand, and the Dartmouth edition notes that a Zephon appears in Scripture only as a man. They find Satan 'Squat like a Toad' at Eve's ear (see the next note). When Ithuriel touches him with his spear, 'no falshood can endure Touch of Celestial temper', and Satan starts up in his own shape. The ensuing exchange is pointed: Satan sneers that not to know him argues themselves unknown; Zephon replies that his lost brightness makes him unrecognisable, 'Thou resembl'st now Thy sin and place of doom obscure and foule' (4.839-40). Satan feels 'how awful goodness is'.

title: Squat like a Toad ... As when a spark Lights on a heap of nitrous Powder
short: Satan whispers Eve's dream in the shape of a toad; touched by Ithuriel's spear he flares up like gunpowder struck by a spark.
body: Satan is found 'Squat like a Toad, close at the eare of Eve', trying to reach 'the Organs of her Fancie' and to taint her 'animal spirits' (the subtle fluids that, in Renaissance physiology, linked body and mind) with dreams of pride; the dream Eve recounts at 5.28-93 is the result. Verity notes Pope's adaptation of the line in his portrait of Sporus in the Epistle to Arbuthnot. When Ithuriel's spear touches him, Satan starts up 'As when a spark Lights on a heap of nitrous Powder', the gunpowder stored in barrels against a rumoured war (4.814-19). Verity records that Tennyson thought this 'the Gunpowder one' and the simile of the ships (2.636-43) the two grandest similes in the poem. Gunpowder points ahead to Satan's invention of cannon in Book VI.

title: Hung forth in Heav'n his golden Scales ... Betwixt Astrea and the Scorpion
short: God weighs the outcome of a fight between Satan and Gabriel in the scales of the constellation Libra; Satan's scale flies up and he flees.
body: As Satan and Gabriel's squadron prepare to fight, God hangs out his 'golden Scales', the constellation Libra, which lies between Virgo ('Astrea', the goddess of justice who left the earth) and Scorpio. Verity traces the image to Homer, where Zeus weighs the fates of Greeks and Trojans (Iliad 8.69-72) and of Achilles and Hector (22.209-13), and to Virgil's weighing of Aeneas and Turnus (Aeneid 12.725-27). Verity shows how Milton varies the model: the scales are those in which God weighed the creation (Isaiah 40:12), and only Satan's own two possible actions, parting or fighting, are weighed. The rising scale shows him 'weigh'd, and shown how light, how weak' (Daniel 5:27, 'Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting'). Satan 'fled Murmuring, and with him fled the shades of night'.
